opus-5.5.text:
I think what excites me most is that it collapses the gap between seeing a place and actually being there. We've had photos, video, and street-level imagery for a long time, but those are all fixed. Someone else chose the angle and the moment, and you can only consume it. When you can step into a generated world grounded in a real location, suddenly you have agency. You can walk down a street, turn a corner, look at something from a perspective nobody has ever captured, and the model fills that in in a way that's consistent with what's really there.

For me there's something almost emotional about that. Think about revisiting the neighborhood you grew up in, or exploring a city you've always wanted to see but haven't been able to travel to. Or even going back in time a bit and imagining what a place looked like decades ago. Anchoring the generation in reality gives it a kind of meaning that a purely imagined world doesn't always have.

From a research perspective it's also a fascinating challenge. A real location constrains the model. It can't just invent anything; it has to respect the geometry, the layout, the character of the place, and stay consistent as you move around and come back to the same spot. That's a really good test of whether these world models are actually building some coherent understanding of the environment, rather than just producing plausible-looking frames.

And then there are the practical directions: education, planning, training agents in environments that resemble the real world, even helping people prepare for a trip or understand a space before they get there. We're still early, and there's a lot to get right in quality, consistency, and responsibility, but the idea that you can take any place on Earth and make it explorable and interactive feels like a genuinely new kind of experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring a generated world grounded in a real location, but does not clearly say that the world can include nonrealistic interactions within that realistic setting.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what excites me most is that it collapses a distinction we've always had to live with. Historically, if you wanted to explore a real place, you either went there physically or you consumed a fixed representation of it: a photo, a video, a 3D scan that someone captured ahead of time. And if you wanted an interactive world, it had to be built by hand, which meant it was almost always fictional or heavily simplified, because building a faithful, explorable copy of a real street or a real landmark is enormously expensive.

Generative world models change that equation. You can take something as simple as a single photograph of a real location, a place you've actually stood, and the model gives you a consistent, navigable environment grounded in that image. You can walk around the corner that wasn't in the frame. You can look up, look behind you. The model is filling in what's plausible given everything it has learned about how the world is structured, while staying anchored to the actual geometry and texture of the place you started from.

What I find compelling about that anchoring is that it's a different thing emotionally than a purely imagined world. There's a reason people care about Street View or about old photographs of their hometown. Real places carry meaning. So being able to step into your childhood neighborhood, or a city you're about to visit, or a historical site as it looked in a specific photo, and move through it rather than just look at it, that feels qualitatively new to me.

And then there's the practical side, which I think is actually underrated. If you want to train agents, robots, or even just test a system in realistic settings, you want environments that reflect the real world's messiness and diversity, not a few hand-built levels. Generating worlds from real-world imagery gives you essentially unlimited, grounded training environments. So it's both this very human, almost nostalgic experience and a genuinely useful technical tool, and I think it's rare that those two things line up so neatly.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring a generated environment grounded in a real location, but does not say that nonrealistic interactions can occur within it.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that a real-world location gives you a starting point that already means something to you. You could start on a street you know, and then imagine what it would feel like to explore a different version of that place. What if the buildings changed? What if you could take a turn and discover something that doesn’t exist today?

And being able to step into that world makes it much more than an image you look at. You’re choosing where to go, and those choices become part of the experience. That connection between something familiar and something you can imagine and explore is really compelling to me.

r001.rationale: It describes starting from a familiar real-world street, changing its buildings and discovering places that do not exist, then actively choosing where to explore in that altered world.

sol-6.1.text: What excites me is that a real place gives you a shared starting point, but it doesn’t have to limit what you can experience. You could start somewhere familiar and then explore how it might look in a different time, or how it could change if you made different choices. And instead of just watching a generated video, you’re there, choosing where to go and what to look at. That ability to participate—to ask “what if?” through exploration—is really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring alternate versions of a familiar real place, but it does not clearly say that nonrealistic interactions can occur within that realistic location.
